documents.title: MFE — Micro-Frontend
documents.contentMarkdown:
# Micro-Frontend (MFE)

Split a web UI into independently built and deployed frontend apps, composed at runtime.

## When to use
- Multiple teams own different parts of one UI
- Independent release cadence per feature area
- Gradual migration of a legacy frontend

## Pros
- Team autonomy & independent deploys
- Tech-stack flexibility per app
- Fault isolation of UI areas

## Cons
- Runtime composition complexity
- Shared design-system / duplication risk
- Larger total payload if not managed

documents.title: BFF — Backend-for-Frontend
documents.contentMarkdown:
# Backend-for-Frontend (BFF)

A dedicated backend per frontend/client that tailors and aggregates APIs for that client's needs.

## When to use
- Different clients (web/mobile) need different payloads
- Reduce chatty calls & over-fetching
- Keep client-specific orchestration out of core services

## Pros
- Optimized payloads per client
- Decouples clients from core services
- Simpler client code

## Cons
- More services to run/deploy
- Possible logic duplication across BFFs
- Extra network hop

documents.title: CQRS — Command Query Responsibility Segregation
documents.contentMarkdown:
# Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS)

Separate the write model (commands) from the read model (queries), often with different stores.

## When to use
- Read and write workloads differ greatly
- Complex domains with rich queries
- Scale reads independently from writes

## Pros
- Independent scaling of reads/writes
- Optimized read models
- Clear separation of concerns

## Cons
- Higher complexity
- Eventual consistency between models
- More infrastructure

documents.title: SAGA — Saga (distributed transaction)
documents.contentMarkdown:
# Saga (distributed transaction) (SAGA)

Coordinate a business transaction across services as a sequence of local steps with compensations.

## When to use
- A transaction spans multiple services
- Two-phase commit is impractical
- Need reliable long-running workflows

## Pros
- No distributed locks
- Failure handling via compensation
- Scales across services

## Cons
- Compensation logic is complex
- Eventual consistency
- Harder to reason about/debug

documents.title: Outbox — Transactional Outbox
documents.contentMarkdown:
# Transactional Outbox (Outbox)

Persist domain changes and outgoing events in the same DB transaction; a relay publishes them reliably.

## When to use
- Need atomic 'update DB + publish event'
- Avoid dual-write inconsistencies
- At-least-once event delivery

## Pros
- No lost events on crash
- Atomic with business data
- Decouples publishing from request path

## Cons
- Relay/poller to operate
- Duplicate delivery (idempotency needed)
- Slight publish latency
